During my years in London I'd seen first-hand how a badly handled PMS migration can genuinely destabilise a whole operation — the Opera to FOLS rollout at Accor was an eye-opener in that respect. I wanted to be on the other side of that equation: implementation, adoption, bridging the gap between what a product promises and what actually happens on the floor. Soho House was a great environment, but it wasn't going to take me there.

No conflict, no problem with the place — it was a deliberate move toward something different.

rows.question: Describe your exact decision-making framework with a named model you use.
rows.answer:
That's not really how I work — I don't operate from named frameworks or methodology models. What I tend to do is more grounded than that.

When I came into the consulting engagement in Galicia, the first move was deliberately not to touch anything. I ran a structured discovery process first — interview scripts, templates, transcripts — specifically to separate what the owner believed was happening from what was actually happening. Those two things were quite different.

From there, the sequencing was roughly: find the leaks before you add anything new, fix what you're already paying for before you buy something else, and make sure whatever you build can be run by someone who isn't you. That last one matters a lot when you're an external collaborator — if the owner can't sustain it, the analysis is worthless.

At HubOS the logic was similar: understand the client's specific situation first, configure to their workflows rather than to a generic template, and measure success by whether staff are actually using the system six weeks after go-live — not by whether the go-live happened.

So there's a pattern there — discovery before action, constraint-first rather than ideal-state thinking, and adoption as the real metric — but I wouldn't give it a name. Named frameworks tend to fit the situation to the model rather than the other way around.
rows.reason: The agent explicitly declined to name a framework, describing instead a general pattern of practice without inventing a specific named methodology.
